sections.title: Problem-Solving Strategy and Setup
sections.content_markdown: The goal of this chapter is to demonstrate the application of kinematic equations to predict the motion of an object. The lecturer emphasizes that while memorizing formulas is common, understanding the underlying assumptions is crucial. To illustrate this, a standard problem is introduced: an object is thrown upward from a building that is 15 meters high with an initial velocity of 10 meters per second. The lecturer defines the origin at the foot of the building and chooses upward as the positive direction. For simplicity, the acceleration due to gravity is approximated as $a = -10$ m/s$^2$ instead of the more precise 9.8 m/s$^2$ to allow for mental calculation. By identifying the initial conditions—initial height $y_0 = 15$ m, initial velocity $v_0 = 10$ m/s, and acceleration $a = -10$ m/s$^2$—we can construct the position equation $y(t) = 15 + 10t - 5t^2$. This equation serves as the complete mathematical description of the object's motion under these specific conditions.

sections.title: Validity and Assumptions
sections.content_markdown: A critical aspect of applying physics formulas is recognizing the domain of their validity. The derived equation $y(t) = 15 + 10t - 5t^2$ is only valid as long as the object is in free fall under the constant acceleration of gravity. If one were to plug in a time like 10,000 seconds, the formula would yield a large negative position, which is physically nonsensical. This occurs because the assumption that the acceleration is constant at $-10$ m/s$^2$ fails once the object hits the ground. Therefore, one must always remember the terms under which a formula was derived. If an answer seems to contradict physical reality, it is essential to revisit the assumptions made during the derivation to ensure they have not been violated. The formula works until the object impacts the ground, at which point the physical situation changes entirely.

sections.title: Determining Velocity
sections.content_markdown: Once the position function $y(t)$ is established, it provides a complete description of the object's location at any given time $t$. To determine how fast the object is moving at any specific moment, we can derive the velocity function from the position function. Since velocity is the rate of change of position with respect to time, we take the derivative of $y(t) = 15 + 10t - 5t^2$. The derivative of this expression with respect to time $t$ gives the velocity function $v(t) = 10 - 10t$. This allows us to calculate the instantaneous velocity of the object at any time $t$ within the valid range of the motion. This process illustrates how kinematic equations are interconnected: once the position is known as a function of time, the velocity can be determined through differentiation, providing a comprehensive view of the object's kinematics.

sections.title: Finding the Maximum Height
sections.content_markdown: To find the maximum height the object reaches, we must identify the specific time $t^*$ when the object is neither moving up nor down. At the highest point of its trajectory, the velocity of the object is exactly zero. Using our velocity function $v(t) = 10 - 10t$, we set $v(t^*) = 0$, which gives $10 - 10t^* = 0$, resulting in $t^* = 1$ second. This tells us the object rises for one second before turning around. To find the maximum height, we substitute this time back into our position equation: $y(1) = 15 + 10(1) - 5(1)^2$. Calculating this gives $y(1) = 15 + 10 - 5 = 20$ meters. This demonstrates how to solve for an unknown variable (maximum height) by using a physical condition (velocity is zero at the peak) to determine the necessary time parameter.

sections.title: Impact Time and Mathematical Solutions
sections.content_markdown: To determine when the object hits the ground, we set the position $y(t)$ to zero, as the ground is defined at $y = 0$ in our coordinate system. This leads to the equation $0 = 15 + 10t - 5t^2$. Simplifying this by dividing by $-5$ yields the quadratic equation $t^2 - 2t - 3 = 0$. Solving for $t$ using the quadratic formula gives $t = \frac{2 \pm \sqrt{4 - 4(1)(-3)}}{2}$, which simplifies to $t = \frac{2 \pm 4}{2}$. This results in two solutions: $t = 3$ seconds and $t = -1$ second. We discard the negative time solution in this context, as the physical event of the object being thrown occurs at $t = 0$. The positive solution, $t = 3$ seconds, represents the time when the object hits the ground.

sections.title: Interpreting Mathematical Results
sections.content_markdown: The appearance of a negative time solution ($t = -1$ s) in the quadratic equation raises the question of why the mathematics provides this result. The mathematical equation $y(t) = 15 + 10t - 5t^2$ is a parabola that does not 'know' about the building or the specific event of throwing a rock. It only knows the initial position, initial velocity, and constant acceleration. The negative solution corresponds to where the parabola would have intersected the ground level ($y=0$) if the motion had been occurring before the clock was set to zero. This highlights that while mathematics is a powerful tool for predicting the future, the results must be interpreted within the context of the physical scenario. Negative time is not inherently wrong, but it must be understood as representing a time before the experiment began, which may or may not be relevant to the specific problem being solved.
